The Humidity *The water vapour present in the atmosphere is known as humidity. Humidity is a result of evaporation of water from the earth surface which reaches the atmosphere. Humidity is expressed in two ways – Absolute Humidity – it is the amount of humidity present in per cubic meter of air at a given temperature. Relative Humidity – it is expressed in percentage. It is the ratio between the total capacity of air to hold moisture at a given temperature and the actual amount of moisture carried. Humidity is directly proportional to the temperature of the air. Humidity decreases from the equator towards poles. Humidity in the tropical region is 2.6% in middle latitudes (50o) it is 0.9% and at 70o latitude and above it is only 0.2%. *90% humidity of the atmosphere is concentrated at an altitude of 5 km from the surface of the earth. 1. So reason (R) is correct. Moisture content decreases with increase in latitude, that is, in tropical region humidity is 2.6%, at 500 latitude it is 0.9% and at 700 latitude it is 0.2% only. The atmosphere contains 90% moisture up to 5 km height from the ground. So the Assertion (A) is also correct. Humidity is directly propositional to temperature, that is at higher temperature air can hold more water vapour than the same amount of air at lower temperatures, so reason (R) is the correct explanation assertion of (A). 2. The Atmospheric Pressure *Air occupies space and has weight. The atmosphere exerts vertical pressure on the earth’s surface. This is called atmospheric pressure. * Atmospheric pressure is measured using a Barometer. It is measured, as the force exerted per unit area of the Barometer. A sudden fall in the level of Barometer is a sign of an upcoming storm. If the readings of a Barometer falls and then starts rising slowly it denotes that there will be rainfall. * A sudden rise in the level of mercury in the Barometer is a sign of an anticyclone and clear weather. * The distribution of atmospheric pressure is shown through an Isobar. * Isobar is an imaginary line that connects points having same atmospheric pressure. *Based on the process of origin, pressure belts can be divided into two parts- (1) Based on thermogenesis – pressure belts thus formed are equatorial low-pressure belts and polar high-pressure belts. (2) Based on Motion-pressure belts thus formed are sub- tropical high-pressure belts and temperate low-pressure belts. *Equatorial Low-Pressure Belts – The belt extends between 5o north and south of Equator. The equator receives vertical rays of the sun all throughout the year. As a result, the air gets heated and starts rising up. Hence the region always experiences low pressure. The surface air of the region moves with very slow velocity as a result of which the environment here is pretty calm. This is the reason this pressure belt is also called Doldrums. z Sub-tropical High-Pressure Belt – the belt is found between 30o-35o latitudes on both the hemispheres. The air rising from the equator starts becoming cooler at the upper layers of atmosphere and hence starts sinking near 30o-35o latitudes. Simultaneously the air from the temperate low- pressure belts also starts descending in this region thus a high-pressure zone is created which gives birth to sub-tropical high pressure belt. The pressure belt is highly mobile in nature, thus it is also called Horse Latitude. z Temperate Low-Pressure Belt – This pressure belt is found between 60o-65o latitudes in both the hemisphere. Though the temperature in this region is low throughout the year yet the region experiences low pressure. It is due to the fact that rotations of the earth cause the air to spread and displaces it. As a result low pressure is created. z Polar High-Pressure Belts – The poles and the regions in close proximity to them experience high pressure because the region is very cold as a result of which air becomes heavy and starts descending creating high pressure. 1. Assertion (A) : 60o–65o latitudes in both the hemispheres have a low-pressure belt instead of high pressure. Reason (R) : The low-pressure areas are stable over oceans rather than on land. Code : (a) Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). (b) Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (c) (A) is true, but (R) is false. (d) (A) is false, but (R) is true. I.A.S. (Pre) 2002 Ans. (c) The sub-polar low-pressure belt lies between 600- 650 latitude in both the hemisphere throughout the year as there is low temperature and low atmospheric pressure. Although this belt has nothing to do with temperature. Hence, assertion (A) is correct. Low atmospheric pressure generally builts upon land whereas high atmospheric pressure builts mostly over oceans. Hence, reason (R) is incorrect. 2. (a) Join−> https://t.me/thehindu000 CB–164 General Studies World Geography The horse latitudes are located at about 30° to 35° north and south of the Equator. In the northern hemisphere it is called as the north sub-tropical high-pressure belt and in the southern hemisphere, it is known as the south sub-tropical high-pressure belt. The existence of these pressure belts is due to the fact that the rising air of the equatorial region is deﬂ ected towards poles due to the earth’s rotation. After becoming cold and heavy, it descends in these regions and get piled up. This results in high pressure. Calm conditions with feeble and variable winds are found here. In ancient times vessels with a cargo of horses passing through these belts found diﬃ culty in sailing under these calm conditions. They used to throw a few horses in the sea in order to make the vessels lighter. Thus, these belts or latitudes came to be known as ‘horse latitudes’. 3. Consider the following statements: 1. (d) Air pressure is defined as the pressure exerted by the weight of air on the earth’s surface. The distribution of air pressure is inﬂ uenced by temperature of air at a given place. Temperature is reversely related with pressure. Due to highest temperature in summer, pressure is lowest on earth. As altitude increases the temperature and air pressure decreases. Distribution of air pressure is influenced by temperature and other kinetic factor (i.e. earth rotation, water vapor, altitude) etc. Clouds *Cloud is a visible dense mass of water droplets or ice crystals suspending in the air. Hence, collectively clouds are a large version of suspend water bodies or glacial bodies. Clouds are found at a relatively higher altitude as compared to fog. *Clouds can be categorized depending upon their shape, vertical expansion and height. Cirrus Clouds – These clouds are found at the highest altitude. These are ﬁ brous and feathery in appearance as they are made up of tiny ice crystals when the rays of the sun pass through these ice crystals the cirrus clouds appear white in colour. They are seen before the advent of a cyclone. Cirro-Stratus Cloud – They are found at an altitude of 1800 feet and above. Their arrival creates a halo around the Sun and the Moon which is a sign of an upcoming cyclone. Cirro-Cumulus Clouds – These clouds are white in appearance and are found in clusters of small ball-shaped patches. Alto-Stratus Clouds – These are those high clouds that are spread across the sky as thin sheets of blue and brown clouds. They are responsible for continuous and expanded rainfall. Alto – Cumulus Clouds – They are low-level clouds just like Cirrocumulus clouds. Strato-Cumulus-Clouds – These are light brown colour clouds often found in big round shaped patches. Stratus Clouds – They are formed as a result of two opposite air bodies, coming in contact with each other. They are often seen during winters in the temperate regions. Nimbo-Stratus Clouds – They are found close to the surface of the Earth. These black clouds are highly dense in nature and can be of any shape. It is because of their highly dense nature that they block the sunlight and make the region dark followed by heavy rainfall. Cumulus Clouds – They are highly dense in nature. Their shape is elongated and the upper portion of them resembles a dome or a cauliﬂ ower. These clouds are the signal of the start of clear weather. Cumulo-Nimbus-Clouds – These clouds are highly diversiﬁ ed and dense in nature. These are a high possibility of rain, hails and thunderstorms associated with these clouds. *Thunder is a process of Thunderstorm. In reality, thunderstorm are local storms in which the air ascends with high velocity. Lighting and thunder is witnessed followed by heavy rainfall. Lighting causes a sudden and high increase in the temperature of the air and there is a sudden expansion in the air leading to thunder. The Winds *The movement of air as a result of the difference in horizontal air pressure is known as Wind. Wind always ﬂ ow from a high- pressure area to a low-pressure area. If the earth was still and ﬂ at the winds would have blown from a high- pressure area directly to a low-pressure area on the Isobaric lines at an angle of 90o. However, the earth is geoid in shape and rotates on its own axis. Hence winds under the inﬂ uence of dynamic forces keep shifting their trajectory. Types of Winds – There are basically three types of wind- Planetary Winds – Winds blowing constantly in a particular direction throughout the year are called Planetary Winds. The main planetary winds are – Trade Winds, Westerlies and Polar Winds. *Trade Winds are winds blowing from sub- tropical high-pressure belt toward equatorial low-pressure belts in both the hemisphere. *Westerlies- They blow from sub-tropical high-pressure belts (30o-35o) towards temperate low-pressure belts (60o-65o) in both the hemisphere. Since there is more landmass in northern Hemisphere as compared to southern Hemisphere the westerlies in the former case are more complex, and they are less inﬂ uential in summers as compared to winter. *Due to the presence of less landmass in the southern hemisphere the westerlies travel at such a high speed that they become stormy. It is because of this high intensity of the westerlies in the southern hemisphere that around 40o latitudes they are known as Roaring Forties, around 50o latitude they are called Furious Fifties and around 60o latitude they are called Shrieking Sixties. *Wellington (New Zealand) is the only Capital in the world that lies in the path of Roaring Forties. *Polar Winds blow from polar high-pressure belt to sub-polar low-pressure belt. The important Periodic Winds are – Monsoonal Winds, Land and Sea Breezes, Breezes of Mountains and Valleys. Monsoonal Winds are those winds which totally reverse their direction as per the seasons. During the six months of summers they blow from sea to land and during the Six months of winters they blow from land to sea. *Land and Sea Breezes only cover 20 to 30 km of the area including the coastal area. During day time the land heats up faster than the nearby sea as a result low pressure is created over land and thus cool and moist winds blow from sea to land. This wind is called Sea Breeze. There is a complete reversal in the direction of the wind during the night. As a result, winds blow from land to sea. This wind is called Land Breeze. z Mountain and Valley Breeze - During day time the air heats up and rises along the slope of the mountain. This is known as valley Breeze. During the night the air gets cooler and heavy as a result it starts descending along the slope of the mountain. This is known as Mountain Breeze. The Local Winds *Local winds are generated as are the result of pressure and temperature gradient in a particular region and hence eﬀ ect a very small area. These winds are conﬁ ned to the lower level of the Troposphere. Important Local Winds are as Follows : *Chinook means ice-eater. These winds blow along the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains and are warm and dry in nature. These winds increase the temperature of the region during winters resulting into melting of ice and the emergence of fresh greenery in the region. The winds rising along the southern slope of Alps descends along the northern slope and is warm and dry in nature. It is called Foehn in Europe and has its maximum inﬂ uence in Switzerland. * Santa Ana is a local wind prevailing in Southern California. It is also a warm and dry wind like Chinook but unlike Chinook, it blows as a Channel Wind in the valley east to west. *Harmattan is a local wind which blow in a North-East and East direction in the eastern parts of Sahara Desert. It is also warm and dry air. With the advent of Harmattan, the weather becomes dry, pleasant and healthy. It is the reason why Harmattan is also called Doctor Wind in the coastal areas of Guinea. *Sirocco is a local wind that blows from the Sahara Desert towards the Mediterranean Sea. The wind is dry, warm and sandy in nature. This air contains a lot of Red Sand.
